segments.text: Welcome to Introduction to Solar System Astronomy. In this brief lesson, we will explore the major bodies orbiting our central star.
At the center of our system is the Sun, an ordinary G-type main-sequence star that contains more than ninety-nine percent of the total mass.
Closest to the Sun are the four terrestrial planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. They are composed primarily of rock and metal.
Mercury is heavily cratered with no substantial atmosphere, while Venus has a dense carbon dioxide atmosphere producing extreme surface heat.
Earth is the only known world with abundant liquid surface water and life, accompanied by its large natural satellite, the Moon.
Mars, the red planet, features ancient river valleys, polar ice caps, and the largest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons.
Separating the inner rocky planets from the outer system is the asteroid belt, populated by thousands of rocky remnants including the dwarf planet Ceres.
Beyond the asteroid belt lie the giant planets. Jupiter is the largest, possessing a turbulent atmosphere with the famous Great Red Spot.
Jupiter also hosts four large Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, each displaying unique geology.
Saturn is famed for its extensive and bright ring system, made largely of ice particles, rocky debris, and dust.
Further out are the ice giants, Uranus and Neptune. Uranus is unique for its extreme axial tilt, rotating essentially on its side.
Neptune is known for its intense supersonic winds, vivid blue appearance from atmospheric methane, and its retrogradely orbiting moon, Triton.
Beyond Neptune's orbit lies the Kuiper belt, a realm of icy bodies and dwarf planets including Pluto, Haumea, and Makemake.
Together, these diverse worlds reveal the dynamic history of accretion, collision, and migration that shaped our cosmic neighborhood.
Thank you for watching this introduction. Continue watching or use WatchMate to pause and explore any concept in detail.
